youtube.title: The Ebola Outbreak Nobody Saw Coming
youtube.description:
In March 2026, three Red Cross volunteers in eastern Congo were asked to bury the dead. It was a routine job, unrelated to Ebola — nobody knew there was an Ebola outbreak, because nobody had found it yet. All three were dead within seven weeks.

The outbreak was not declared until 15 May. As of 17 August the CDC reports 5,105 confirmed cases and 2,420 confirmed deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It is spreading substantially faster than any Ebola outbreak on record: it passed 1,000 confirmed cases 40 days after the response was activated, against roughly 235 days for the 2018 outbreak in the same country. CDC calls it the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record.

The reason everyone has reported is that there is no vaccine. That is true, and it is not the reason.

There is an Ebola vaccine — Ervebo — and it works. It is licensed against Zaire ebolavirus. This outbreak is a different species, Bundibugyo, seen only twice before and both times contained. CEPI puts it plainly: there are no licensed vaccines for Bundibugyo virus.

But containing Ebola has never depended on a vaccine. It depends on administration — finding every contact, visiting each daily for 21 days, isolating anyone who develops a fever. Every step assumes you can locate someone, reach them safely, and that they open the door. In eastern Congo each assumption fails independently: 4.4 million internally displaced people, years of armed conflict, responders briefly detained, facilities attacked. The CDC lists violence against health workers, shortages of protective equipment, and lack of trust in government and misinformation among the reasons the response is failing. The World Food Programme counted 8.7 million people at crisis levels of hunger in these provinces before Ebola arrived.

The absent vaccine is the headline. The absent administrative and security capacity is the cause.

A NOTE ON RISK
Ebola is not airborne and does not spread by casual contact. The CDC has confirmed no cases in the United States from this outbreak and puts the risk to the American public at low. A case fatality rate describes people diagnosed with a disease in the places it is spreading. It does not describe your risk. Outside the region there has been one confirmed exported case, in France.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The burial nobody connected to Ebola
0:43 What is actually happening
2:02 What that number does not mean
2:52 The headline
3:37 What you do when there is no vaccine
4:16 Why that fails here
5:42 The seven weeks
6:23 What happens now

SOURCES
• CDC, Ebola Outbreak: Current Situation, 20 Aug 2026 — all case and death figures in this film. DRC as of 17 Aug; Uganda and France as of 18 Aug. Also the second-largest-on-record framing, the 40-days-vs-235-days comparison, and the response-challenge list. https://www.cdc.gov/ebola/situation-summary/index.html
• The first-100-days chart is redrawn from the data table CDC publishes beneath its own chart (Data Sources: DRC INSP, WHO; DRC data as of 19 Aug 2026). It compares EARLY GROWTH, not total outbreak size.
• WHO Disease Outbreak News DON615, 12 Aug 2026 — 54 health zones, 6 provinces. https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2026-DON615
• CEPI — "There are no licensed vaccines for Bundibugyo virus." https://cepi.net/bundibugyo-virus-what-it-and-what-it-not
• CDC, History of Ebola Outbreaks — the 2014-16 and 2018-20 comparisons. https://www.cdc.gov/ebola/outbreaks/index.html
• IFRC, 23 May 2026 — the three volunteers, DRC Red Cross Mongbwalu branch. https://www.ifrc.org/article/statement-ifrc-saddened-deaths-three-drc-red-cross-volunteers-ituri-province
• UN News, May 2026 (4.4m displaced; WHO DG on tracing) • OCHA, 27 Jul 2026 (responders detained) • US State Dept, 5 Aug 2026 ($512m) • CNN, 22 May 2026 (aid cuts) • WFP (hunger).

WHAT WE LEFT OUT, AND WHY
Two institutions publish different totals for the same week. WHO AFRO, via UN News on 18 August, gave 5,021 cases and 2,378 deaths; CDC, reporting DRC health-ministry data as of 17 August, gives 5,105 and 2,420 — a higher figure on an earlier date. Neither is wrong: DRC excludes probable cases from official reporting and has temporarily excluded suspected ones pending investigation, so national surveillance and WHO's validated regional figures run on different clocks. This film uses CDC's numbers throughout, on one basis, with the date on screen.

We make no claim that the virus is mutating or becoming more lethal: the case fatality rate rose from 44% on 30 July to 47.4% on 17 August, and that can reflect improved counting. No death-toll projection. No causal line drawn between aid cuts and case counts — the commitment figure and the reported criticism sit side by side, attributed. No identifiable patient appears at any point.

All footage is real. No AI-generated imagery is used in this video.
